findings.description: `refund()` applies the fraction of pieces not sent to a byte-based allowance, even though the last piece can be much shorter than the others. For a 65,537-byte file, if the first 65,536-byte piece leaves but the one-byte tail fails, the sender refunds half the allowance and can admit further requests after transmitting almost the entire file.
findings.title: Stalled sends can exceed the byte limit

evidence.explanation: `askBytes` charges a whole-file request by file size, and the limiter stores that charge as bytes. `sendFile` instead reports counts of successful pieces and total pieces; the new refund helper converts those counts into a fraction of the stored byte charge. With one full piece sent and a one-byte tail unsent, it therefore refunds substantially more than the one unsent byte.

findings.description: `onMessage` records each whole-file retry with `asks.allow` before `sendFile` can transmit, and a failed send does not restore the allowance. If a connection cannot send any bytes during the first three requests but recovers within the minute, the receiver’s subsequent retries are dropped until the window expires, by which time its retry budget can be exhausted.
findings.title: Recovered transfers still fail

evidence.explanation: The work-ticket skill calls for checking callers when a change makes work fail that previously waited or succeeded. The new gate records an allowance before sending, while the receiver continues issuing whole-file retries after silence and has a finite retry budget; the send path can fail while waiting for a usable connection.

findings.description: `askLimiter.allow()` deletes the oldest counter when all 2,000 records are live, discarding its whole-send history before the 60-second window expires. In a room with enough device-and-file combinations, the affected device can request that file again immediately, and further live-record evictions can repeatedly restore its quota.
findings.title: Busy rooms can reset a device’s send limit

evidence.explanation: Records are keyed per device and file, and the three-send check consults only the record still in the map. The cap removes the oldest record without checking whether it remains live, so its next request creates a fresh record with an empty send history; unlike the stale-record test, a room can fill the cap with live combinations.
